papers.title: KVStream: Adaptive Parallel Storage Management for KV Caching in Large-Scale LLM Serving
papers.authors: Avinash Maurya, Jaiaid Mobin, Jie Ye, M. Mustafa Rafique, Franck Cappello, Bogdan Nicolae
papers.abstract: Long-context LLM serving for agentic, coding, and document workloads reuses prefixes whose key-value (KV) cache outgrows GPU and host memory, putting storage I/O on the critical path of the inference step for retrieving prefixes. A single node-local NVMe absorbs all retrievals, while the parallel file system or cloud file store that nodes already mount carries almost no inference traffic. We cast prefix retrieval as aggregate-bandwidth scheduling across these tiers and present KVStream, a KV cache engine that batches a step's reads, defers writes behind the forward pass, replicates each chunk on every tier, and lets each tier adaptively claim the next unread chunks once it is free. Our performance model shows this routing attains the aggregate-bandwidth bound without prediction or tuning, whereas any static split misses it by a margin that grows as per-tier bandwidths drift or fluctuate. It also predicts that the time-to-first-token (TTFT) gain grows with load, as faster retrieval drains the queue, and disappears when host memory or arrival order keeps reuse in cache. Plugged into LMCache and evaluated on four models, six datasets, and up to 128 GPUs, KVStream retrieves within 5% of the bound, delivers up to 1.49$\times$ higher offline throughput than LMCache, and lowers mean TTFT by up to 6.1$\times$ under bursty arrivals.

Existing systems read only from the node-local NVMe, while the parallel file system that every cluster already mounts sits almost idle. Plugged into LMCache, ==it reaches up to 1.49x LMCache's offline throughput and up to 6.1x lower mean TTFT under bursty traffic==.

My verdict: teams running long-context inference services, especially multi-turn agent and coding-assistant workloads, should read this. Its value is not a new algorithm but a very practical observation: GPU nodes already have a second storage path next to them, and nobody uses it during inference. The method is simple, too. It needs no prediction of which prefixes will be reused and no tuning of split ratios. The cost is that every KV chunk is written twice, so it only pays off when reads dominate writes, and the paper measures the cases where it gets slower.

## What problem is it solving?

First, the setting. Inference engines (vLLM, SGLang) cache the KV of prefixes they have computed, so a later request that shares the prefix does not recompute it. LMCache is an open-source KV cache connector. It cuts the KV that does not fit into chunks of 256 tokens, stores them in host memory and on local disk, and reads them back to the GPU on a hit.

The trouble is that the total volume of prefixes is huge. Each test node has 4 GPUs with about 140 GB left for KV after model weights, plus 512 GB of host memory. For a 14B model, the unique prefixes to cache across several document datasets are 0.5 to 1 TB, 3.3 to 7.2 times what the GPUs can hold. For a 110B model the volume approaches 2 TB. So most prefixes can only live on disk.

![Figure 5 of the paper: LMCache's timeline for one inference step on a 70B model. The step batches 7 requests; each request's storage reads (600 to 1300 ms) queue up one after another, and the step spends 4.7 seconds on disk reads alone.](figs/2610.31827/m5_retrieval_serialization_v2.png)

How slow are the reads? The figure above is a concrete case: one step of a 70B model holds 7 requests, LMCache reads them one request at a time, each takes 600 to 1300 ms, and the step spends 4.7 seconds just reading. Worse, the forward pass cannot start until the KV of every request in the step has arrived, so finishing one request early gains nothing. On LooGLE, disk reads account for 80% to 88% of LMCache's total time at all four model sizes. Even so, reading from disk still beats recomputing, by up to 2.2x on large models, because recompute cost grows with model depth while read cost grows only with bytes.

## Why the local disk alone is not enough

The authors first run a set of measurements with three findings.

First, the second path sits idle. GPU nodes in supercomputing clusters and in the cloud usually mount a shared parallel file system (PFS below, such as Lustre or a managed cloud file system). Measured alone, the local NVMe reads only 2.2x (testbed 1) and 3.2x (testbed 2) faster than the PFS. Yet during inference the PFS carries almost no traffic beyond loading model weights, so its bandwidth is effectively free.

Second, reads and writes on the same disk interfere. The new KV from each step has to be written while the old KV needed by the next step is read from the same disk. Doing 512 GB of reads and 512 GB of writes concurrently takes 6% (testbed 1) and 27% (testbed 2) longer than doing them separately. So any split of reads based on idle-time bandwidth is wrong once inference is actually running.

Third, per-chunk latency has a long tail. On testbed 2, isolated NVMe reads have a median of 123 ms and a P99 of 216 ms; with reads and writes mixed, the P99 rises to 898 ms. The PFS has a 102 ms median but a 795 ms P99, because every job in the cluster shares it. The bandwidth each tier can deliver keeps changing from one inference step to the next.

## KVStream's four changes

![Figure 4 of the paper: (a) many compute nodes share one parallel file system. (b) Inside a node, 4 GPUs reach the local NVMe and the parallel file system over two non-overlapping paths. (c) Within one forward pass, prefix writes for step i interleave with prefix reads for step i+1, and all GPUs on the node compete for both tiers.](figs/2610.31827/arch.png)

KVStream makes four changes to address these problems.

The first change is reading the whole step at once. Instead of reading one request at a time, it puts every chunk that the step's requests need into one read queue and submits them together. NVMe only reaches full speed with many reads in flight, and a one-at-a-time queue wastes that parallelism. Each chunk is also shipped to the GPU the moment it arrives.

The second change is deferring writes. Newly computed KV is held in host memory and written to disk only after the next forward pass starts. The disks are idle for reads during the forward pass, so writes rarely block reads.

The third change is writing every chunk twice. Each KV chunk is stored on both the local NVMe and the PFS. Any chunk can then be read from any tier, with no need to guess in advance which chunks will be needed or where to put them. Storage capacity is usually measured in terabytes, so a second copy is rarely a problem; the cost is twice the bytes written.

The fourth change is reading from both ends toward the middle, with the faster tier reading more. The step's chunks form a list; the NVMe reads from the front and the PFS from the back, m chunks at a time. Whichever tier finishes its current batch immediately claims the next one, and the two meet somewhere in the middle. The faster tier naturally reads more and the slower one less, with no bandwidth measurement and no ratio to tune. A few chunks near the meeting point may be read by both; since the content is identical, the first copy is used and the other is dropped.

In implementation terms, KVStream is a C++ library that does asynchronous reads and writes with io_uring, using separate queues for reads and writes, and plugs into LMCache as a storage backend. Engines like vLLM that already use LMCache need no code changes.

## Meeting in the middle: a worked example

Why not just use a fixed split, say 75% from NVMe and 25% from the PFS? The paper gives an example, worked through here.

Suppose a step must read 12 GB, the NVMe reads at 3 GB/s and the PFS at 1 GB/s. Together that is 4 GB/s, so the fastest possible time is 3 seconds; this is what the paper calls the aggregate-bandwidth bound. With a 75:25 split, the NVMe reads 9 GB in 3 seconds and the PFS reads 3 GB in 3 seconds, finishing together.

Now the NVMe slows to 2 GB/s because it is also absorbing writes. Under the fixed split it needs 4.5 seconds for its 9 GB while the PFS sits idle. The combined bandwidth is 3 GB/s, so the bound is 4 seconds, and the fixed split is 12.5% slower. If instead the PFS is squeezed by another job down to 0.5 GB/s, its 3 GB take 6 seconds, slower than reading all 12 GB from the NVMe alone (4 seconds).

Meeting in the middle avoids this. Whichever side slows down, the meeting point shifts toward it, and both sides finish at about the same time. A simple model in the paper shows that this routing stays at the aggregate-bandwidth bound in every step, apart from the last batch of m chunks. ==A fixed split is optimal only when the bandwidth ratio happens to equal the split ratio, and loses as soon as bandwidth shifts==, which it does constantly during inference.

## How the experiments are set up

There are two supercomputing testbeds: testbed 1 has 4 H100s per node, testbed 2 has 4 A100s per node, each mounts a shared file system, and each node has local NVMe. Four models from 14B to 110B are used, all with TP=4, covering both the case where recompute is cheap and the case where reading is cheap.

Offline tests use three long-document datasets: LooGLE (long-document QA), NarrativeQA (whole-book reading comprehension, 46K tokens per request on average) and CUAD (legal clause extraction). Online tests replay three real traces: about 7,000 requests from a Qwen code-generation cluster on Alibaba Cloud Bailian, agent sessions from the Chutes platform, and coding-agent sessions on SWE-bench. In these workloads 80% to 96% of prompt tokens hit a cached prefix.

Baselines are: GPU plus host memory only, recomputing on a miss ("memory only" below); LMCache with local NVMe; Mooncake's KV store; and SGLang's built-in hierarchical cache HiCache. LMCache is the strongest baseline and most comparisons use it.

## Result 1: offline throughput

| Model | Throughput vs LMCache |
|---|---:|
| 14B | 1.17x |
| 32B | 1.37x |
| 70B | 1.48x |
| 110B | 1.49x |

![Figure 16 of the paper: offline throughput on LooGLE on testbed 1, by model size. KVStream is above both LMCache and the memory-only baseline at every size, and the gap widens as the model grows.](figs/2610.31827/g01_model_scaling_throughput_v2.png)

On LooGLE, the larger the model, the larger KVStream's advantage. There are two reasons: a larger model has more KV per token, so fewer prefixes fit in memory and more reads go to disk; and recompute cost grows with depth faster than KV size does, since the 70B model has 5 times the parameters of the 14B one but only twice the KV per token.

Read bandwidth explains the gain. On one node LMCache reads 6.0 to 6.7 GB/s from the NVMe; KVStream reads about the same from the NVMe and another 2.8 to 4.9 GB/s from the PFS, 8.1 to 11.8 GB/s in total. Both read about the same total volume from disk, so the speedup comes entirely from parallel reads. Across datasets, the 32B model gains only 1.05x on CUAD, because CUAD requests are the shortest, 11K tokens on average, so disk reads are a smaller share of each step.

## Result 2: how much a fixed split loses

![Figure 21 of the paper: 32B model on LooGLE on testbed 2. The horizontal axis is the share of storage reads the NVMe actually serves, the vertical axis is how far each run is above the aggregate-bandwidth bound. Fixed splits (orange) form a V; even the best is 8% slower and the worst nearly 68%. KVStream (green square) sits at the bound.](figs/2610.31827/eval_bound_share.png)

The authors test the previous section's argument on testbed 2 with the 32B model. On a file system with no other jobs, the fixed split's distance from the bound is V-shaped: best when the split matches the average bandwidth ratio, yet still 8.0% slower, and up to 67.7% slower when the split is off. KVStream has no ratio to tune and stays within 4.3% of the bound. Even the best fixed ratio only matches on average, because bandwidth changes every step.

Then another job pushes periodic, bursty or steady traffic onto the PFS, simulating other cluster users. Now even the best fixed split is 11.8% to 23.6% slower, while KVStream stays within 4.3%. As long as someone else is using the shared storage, a fixed ratio loses, however well it was tuned.

## Result 3: in online serving, queueing amplifies small gains

Online, the metric is TTFT, which is a request's own processing time plus the time it waits behind earlier requests. Faster reads not only finish the current batch sooner but also let queued requests start sooner, so the gain grows with load.

On the SWE-bench coding-agent trace, with a 1-second TTFT target, 84% of requests meet it with KVStream and 70% with LMCache; every other baseline is below 55%. The speedup from reading a second tier is something users feel directly.

On the code-generation trace, as the arrival rate goes from low to medium to high, KVStream's mean-TTFT speedup over LMCache grows from 1.07x to 1.61x to 3.12x. Per request, though, it spends only 15% to 22% less time reading than LMCache. The difference is the queue: at high load LMCache has 128 requests waiting on average, KVStream 54.3. So the big TTFT improvement comes mostly from draining the queue faster, not from any single read.

![Figure 14 of the paper: on the SWE-bench coding-agent trace, mean TTFT (bars) and P90 TTFT (lines) for each method as arrivals get burstier (horizontal axis: coefficient of variation of inter-arrival times). KVStream is lowest at every level, with its largest advantage over LMCache at a coefficient of 4.](figs/2610.31827/o2_burstiness_v2.png)

The burstier the traffic, the stronger the queueing effect. Burstiness is measured by the coefficient of variation of inter-arrival times, about 4.3 for real production traffic. At a coefficient of 4, KVStream's mean TTFT is 6.07x lower than LMCache's; at an extreme 8, beyond real traffic, the advantage shrinks to 1.17x.

It also holds at scale. On testbed 2, from 4 to 32 nodes (128 GPUs), each replica has its own NVMe but all share one PFS. KVStream keeps a 1.23x to 1.36x throughput advantage over LMCache at every scale, because each node routes its own reads by completion and reads more from local disk when the PFS is congested, with no coordination between nodes.

## When it does not help, or gets slower

This is the part I find most useful, because the authors measured the cases where their own method loses.

First, it does not help when host memory is big enough. On the Chutes trace, raising host memory from 40 GB to 80 GB per GPU lets almost every reuse hit in memory, and disk reads drop by 98.6%. KVStream is then 0.98x of LMCache, slightly slower, because it still writes a second copy.

Second, request order decides how much must be read. On the same code-generation trace, if a session's turns arrive close together, most prefixes are still in memory and KVStream is only 1.05x faster. If many sessions interleave in turn, each turn is separated by lots of other KV, and it is 3.12x faster. Online services usually must process requests in arrival order rather than reorder them for cache hits, so the second case is the common one.

Third, it gets slower when reuse is low. The authors artificially lower prefix reuse on the SWE-bench trace: at 88% reuse KVStream is 6.0x faster, at 77% the two are even (0.97x), and at 4% it is only 0.81x. Less reuse means more new KV to write and less to read back, so the cost of writing twice outweighs the gain from parallel reads.

## What each change contributes

| Configuration | Offline throughput (tokens/s, 70B) | Online mean TTFT (s, 32B) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Memory only | 18513 | 340.7 |
| LMCache (local NVMe) | 31977 | 31.1 |
| + whole-step reads | 32115 | 20.2 |
| + deferred writes | 32177 | 19.8 |
| + second tier, fixed split | 39631 | 122.1 |
| + faster tier reads more (full KVStream) | 47210 | 13.0 |

Offline throughput comes almost entirely from the second tier: with a single NVMe, its bandwidth is the cap however reads and writes are scheduled, and the first two changes move throughput by less than 1%. Adding the PFS with a fixed 70:30 split brings throughput to 1.24x LMCache, and routing by completion brings it to 1.48x.

The online column has a counterintuitive result: the fixed split pushes TTFT to 122.1 seconds, far worse than LMCache. In this online run the fixed split keeps no second copy: the first 80% of each prefix's chunks live only on the NVMe and the last 20% only on the PFS. A fixed split decides each chunk's tier when it is written and never moves it. The chunks a new turn appends are always at the very end of the prefix at that moment, which by position falls in the last 20%, so most newly written chunks live only on the PFS. The PFS ends up serving 47% of reads with only 15% of the bandwidth and becomes the bottleneck. In multi-tier storage, assigning data in advance by position or ratio goes wrong easily; assigning at read time is what stays robust.

## Limitations as I see them

First, doubling the write volume is a real cost. The authors tried two compromises in their simulator. Adding a replica only after a tier slows down cuts writes to 1.19x, but reads end up 12% to 74% above the bound, because the replica arrives after the step has already stalled. Replicating only part of each prefix's chunks (a fixed 40%) costs 1.43x writes and reads at most 5% above the bound. So if your storage is short on write bandwidth, partial replication is the direction to try first.

Second, the gain depends heavily on workload shape. It suits long prompts, short outputs, many interleaved sessions and working sets that do not fit in memory. With long outputs, decoding dilutes the share of disk reads and Amdahl's law caps the speedup: from 16 to 256 output tokens, the offline advantage stays between 1.19x and 1.37x.

Third, all experiments are on supercomputing clusters whose shared storage is a dedicated high-performance parallel file system. A managed cloud file system or object store may behave very differently in bandwidth and latency, so measure your own. Nodes also do not coordinate, so the same prefix may be stored on the PFS once per node, wasting capacity and write bandwidth; the authors leave cross-node sharing to future work.

## How a team could try it

1. First confirm that disk reads are your bottleneck: measure the share of each step spent reading KV from disk. If host memory already holds most reused prefixes, this will not help.
2. Check whether nodes have a second independent storage path, such as a shared file system, a second NVMe or remote NVMe, and measure each one's read and write bandwidth under inference load.
3. If you already use LMCache, integration is cheapest. Otherwise the scheduling rule itself, reading from both ends and letting whoever finishes first claim the next batch, is easy to port into your own KV storage layer.
4. Before launch, replay your own real traffic and watch TTFT at peak and under bursts, and whether low-reuse workloads get slower.

## Bottom line

==The disk-read bottleneck of long-context KV caching does not necessarily need a faster disk: use the idle shared storage in the cluster as well, let each tier claim work at its actual speed, and reads stay close to the aggregate-bandwidth bound.==

| Dimension | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Importance of the problem | High. Long agent and coding sessions push KV cache far beyond memory, and disk reads are now the bottleneck |
| Novelty | Medium. No single mechanism is new, but the combination plus the performance model explains things clearly |
| Experimental evidence | High. 4 models, 6 datasets, up to 128 GPUs, including the cases where it gets slower |
| Engineering cost | Medium-low. Plugs in as an LMCache backend with no engine changes; doubles write volume |
| Worth trying? | Yes. Inference services with long sessions, many interleaved users and working sets beyond memory should evaluate it first |

The authors test the previous section's argument on testbed 2 with the 32B model. On a file system with no other jobs, the fixed split's distance from the bound is V-shaped: best when the split matches the average bandwidth ratio, yet still 8.0% slower, and up to 67.7% slower when the split is off. Then another job pushes periodic, bursty or steady traffic onto the PFS, simulating other cluster users. Now even the best fixed split is 11.8% to 23.6% slower, while KVStream stays within 4.3%. As long as someone else is using the shared storage, a fixed ratio loses, however well it was tuned.

Result 3: in online serving, queueing amplifies small gains

Online, the metric is TTFT, which is a request's own processing time plus the time it waits behind earlier requests. Faster reads not only finish the current batch sooner but also let queued requests start sooner, so the gain grows with load.

On the SWE-bench coding-agent trace, with a 1-second TTFT target, 84% of requests meet it with KVStream and 70% with LMCache; every other baseline is below 55%. The speedup from reading a second tier is something users feel directly.

On the code-generation trace, as the arrival rate goes from low to medium to high, KVStream's mean-TTFT speedup over LMCache grows from 1.07x to 1.61x to 3.12x. Per request, though, it spends only 15% to 22% less time reading than LMCache. The difference is the queue: at high load LMCache has 128 requests waiting on average, KVStream 54.3. So the big TTFT improvement comes mostly from draining the queue faster, not from any single read.

The burstier the traffic, the stronger the queueing effect. Burstiness is measured by the coefficient of variation of inter-arrival times, about 4.3 for real production traffic. At a coefficient of 4, KVStream's mean TTFT is 6.07x lower than LMCache's; at an extreme 8, beyond real traffic, the advantage shrinks to 1.17x.

KVStream keeps a 1.23x to 1.36x throughput advantage over LMCache at every scale, because each node routes its own reads by completion and reads more from local disk when the PFS is congested, with no coordination between nodes.

When it does not help, or gets slower

This is the part I find most useful, because the authors measured the cases where their own method loses.

First, it does not help when host memory is big enough. On the Chutes trace, raising host memory from 40 GB to 80 GB per GPU lets almost every reuse hit in memory, and disk reads drop by 98.6%. KVStream is then 0.98x of LMCache, slightly slower, because it still writes a second copy.

Second, request order decides how much must be read. On the same code-generation trace, if a session's turns arrive close together, most prefixes are still in memory and KVStream is only 1.05x faster. If many sessions interleave in turn, each turn is separated by lots of other KV, and it is 3.12x faster. Online services usually must process requests in arrival order rather than reorder them for cache hits, so the second case is the common one.

Third, it gets slower when reuse is low. The authors artificially lower prefix reuse on the SWE-bench trace: at 88% reuse KVStream is 6.0x faster, at 77% the two are even (0.97x), and at 4% it is only 0.81x. Less reuse means more new KV to write and less to read back, so the cost of writing twice outweighs the gain from parallel reads.

Offline throughput comes almost entirely from the second tier: with a single NVMe, its bandwidth is the cap however reads and writes are scheduled, and the first two changes move throughput by less than 1%. Adding the PFS with a fixed 70:30 split brings throughput to 1.24x LMCache, and routing by completion brings it to 1.48x.

In this online run the fixed split keeps no second copy: the first 80% of each prefix's chunks live only on the NVMe and the last 20% only on the PFS. A fixed split decides each chunk's tier when it is written and never moves it. The chunks a new turn appends are always at the very end of the prefix at that moment, which by position falls in the last 20%, so most newly written chunks live only on the PFS. The PFS ends up serving 47% of reads with only 15% of the bandwidth and becomes the bottleneck. In multi-tier storage, assigning data in advance by position or ratio goes wrong easily; assigning at read time is what stays robust.

Limitations as I see them

First, doubling the write volume is a real cost. The authors tried two compromises in their simulator. Second, the gain depends heavily on workload shape. It suits long prompts, short outputs, many interleaved sessions and working sets that do not fit in memory. The disk-read bottleneck of long-context KV caching does not necessarily need a faster disk: use the idle shared storage in the cluster as well, let each tier claim work at its actual speed, and reads stay close to the aggregate-bandwidth bound.

papers.summary: By moving generative podcast recommendation off two separate inference engines and onto TensorRT-LLM together with NVIDIA, Spotify cut beam search cost by up to 54% and scoring cost by up to 7% on Qwen3-1.7B. deep_reading.title: Advancing Generative Recommendation Inference: our collaboration with NVIDIA on TensorRT LLM
deep_reading.content:
Spotify runs generative podcast recommendation with semantic IDs, and a single online request needs three kinds of inference: beam search to generate candidates, scoring a given batch of candidates, and inserting the user vector into the prompt as one soft token. These used to be split across two inference engines, vLLM and SGLang, and vLLM's beam search could not saturate the GPU, so Spotify fell back to lower-tier cards. Spotify and NVIDIA added the missing features to TensorRT-LLM and unified all three in one engine. ==On Qwen3-1.7B, beam search cost drops by up to 54% and scoring cost by up to 7%==.

My verdict: teams that have shipped or plan to ship generative recommendation should read this. It is not a methods paper but a very concrete engineering record: the inference features generative recommendation needs are quite different from chat, and the mainstream open-source engines each support only part of them. The post breaks the requirements down clearly and shows throughput comparisons after closing the gaps. The most useful part is the three requirements themselves, which almost every team using semantic IDs for retrieval and LLMs for ranking will run into.

## Background: what inference a recommendation request needs

In January 2026 Spotify launched LLM-based generative retrieval for podcast recommendations. The approach follows PLUM (a paper that adapts pre-trained LLMs into generative recommenders): each podcast is represented by a short string of semantic IDs, the model reads the user information and generates that code one token at a time, and the generated code is mapped back to a podcast.

![Figure from the Spotify post: turning a user vector into a soft token. Step 1, the prompt holds a placeholder token, and next to it is the user vector fetched from the embedding store. Step 2, ordinary tokens are looked up in the vocabulary as usual, while the user vector goes through a learned linear projection into the model's hidden size and replaces the placeholder's slot. Step 3, the first forward pass runs with this personalized token, so the output reflects the user's preferences.](figs/web_spotify-tensorrt-inference/softtoken.png)

To turn this into a service across many surfaces, the inference engine has to support three things at once.

The first is beam search. Generating a code cannot follow only the single most likely path; it keeps several of the highest-scoring prefixes, expands and prunes at each step, and the complete codes left at the end are the candidate podcasts. So the engine must not only support beam search but return the results of multiple beams, not just the best one.

The second is candidate scoring. Sometimes the candidates already exist and the LLM only has to judge which are better. The candidates go into the prompt, the model's log probabilities for label tokens such as "yes" or "no" are read out, and the candidates are ranked by them.

The third is personalization. Recommendations must know who is listening, and Spotify already has a mature set of dense user embeddings. How to hand that vector to the LLM is another feature the engine has to support.

## Why beam search could not saturate the GPU in vLLM

The January launch used vLLM. It is one of the most widely used open-source inference engines and handles ordinary completion requests very well, but its beam search is weaker. The post names two reasons. First, vLLM implements beam search outside the core GPU engine, so much of the scheduling falls on the CPU and the CPU becomes the bottleneck. Second, it recomputes partially filled KV blocks, adding extra GPU work. My reading: because beam search lives outside the engine, each expansion step effectively resubmits every beam as a new request; vLLM's prefix cache only reuses full KV blocks, so the tokens already in the last, partially filled block of each beam are recomputed at every step.

As a result, high-end GPUs sat underused. To control cost, Spotify launched on lower-tier cards and kept the system at a better load point. This is a typical trade-off: if the engine cannot saturate high-end cards, cheaper cards give a lower unit cost.

## Scoring many candidates at once

The most direct way to score candidates is to fan out: send one request per candidate, read each one's label probabilities, and aggregate. More candidates means more requests, and the same user prefix is computed over and over.

![Figure from the Spotify post: multi-item scoring. Step 1, the user prefix (system prompt, profile, history) and N candidates are joined with delimiters into one sequence, and the user prefix's KV is computed once. Step 2, an attention mask isolates the candidates so each sees only the user prefix and itself, never the other candidates. Step 3, the log probabilities of the "yes" and "no" labels are read at the end of each candidate, converted to a score, and ranked.](figs/web_spotify-tensorrt-inference/scoring.png)

SGLang has a more efficient approach, which LinkedIn's engineering team also contributed to; call it multi-item scoring. The figure shows it clearly: the user prefix and all candidates are joined into one sequence, an attention mask lets each candidate see only the user prefix and itself, and a single forward pass scores every candidate. This avoids the overhead of one request per candidate while keeping compute linear in the number of candidates. That is why Spotify used SGLang for scoring.

## Getting the user vector into the prompt: three approaches

The post compares three ways of giving user information to the LLM, which is very useful for anyone building LLM-based recommendation.

The first is to write the user's listening and interaction history as text in the prompt. Describing a user accurately takes a lot of text, and long prompts push latency beyond the request budget and raise GPU usage. So this is used sparingly, for example only for the user's most recent real-time streams.

The second is to give users semantic IDs too, as in PLUM: tokens representing users are added to the vocabulary, a handful of tokens stand for a user, prompts stay short, and inference needs no special support. The model is fine-tuned with the extended vocabulary. Early results were promising, but the post says this path needs more experimentation and is not in production yet.

The third works best: soft tokens, from Spotify Research's "Embedding to Prefix" method. The idea is to learn a projection that maps the existing user vector into the LLM's embedding space as a single token-sized vector. Fine-tuning trains two parts together: the projection layer (one linear layer) is learned end to end, and the LLM itself updates only a subset of its weights so it learns to use the vector. At inference the user vector is projected, inserted into the prompt, and then the first forward pass runs. The figure above shows the process. Podcast recommendation uses this method, and Spotify is extending it to other tasks on its internal LLM.

The benefit is reusing years of user embeddings from the recommender without lengthening the prompt. The cost is that the engine must let you replace the vector at one position before the forward pass, while most engines accept only token IDs by default.

## Moving all three into TensorRT-LLM

After the launch, generative recommendation is expanding from podcasts to more content and surfaces, so an efficient, maintainable inference stack matters more. The goal of the Spotify and NVIDIA collaboration was clear: unify efficient beam search, scoring and user soft tokens in one engine.

TensorRT-LLM had better hardware utilization for beam search but initially lacked two things: a scoring API like SGLang's, and soft-token injection plus multi-beam result return like vLLM's. The two teams added the following, all now in released versions:

| New feature | First version | Need it serves |
|---|---|---|
| Beam search returns multiple sequences | v1.2.0rc3 | Generative retrieval needs several candidate codes |
| trtllm-serve supports out-of-tree models | v1.2.0rc4 | Plug in your own model extension |
| Multimodal embeddings via the image_embeds parameter | v1.3.0rc0 | A path for passing user vectors |
| Multi-item scoring in the Python API | v1.3.0rc20 | Score a batch of candidates in one forward pass |

In TensorRT-LLM, beam search is implemented inside the sampler, which cuts CPU-side overhead, and together with overlap scheduling (the GPU keeps working while the CPU prepares the next step) it gets better GPU utilization. The old C++ sampler was also replaced by a more flexible design that relies more on PyTorch, and beam search on the new sampler is notably faster than before.

Soft tokens are built on out-of-tree model support. With NVIDIA's help, Spotify wrote a Qwen3 extension plugin: the user vector comes in through multimodal request parameters, and the plugin does the projection and replaces the placeholder token. This is a neat trick, because multimodal models already have to insert image vectors into the prompt, and reusing that path avoids touching the engine core.

Scoring got an extension to the Python API equivalent to SGLang's scoring API. For now, a custom serving layer is still needed for efficient tokenization and request batching.

## Performance: how to read the two benchmark charts

![Figure from the Spotify post: latency and throughput for beam search with beam width 30, TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc21 (blue) vs vLLM 0.26.0 (purple), on an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition, with 2,000-token prompts and only 5 decoded tokens. The left two panels plot latency against achieved QPS; the right panel shows saturation QPS, 33.2 vs 15.0 for the 1.7B model and 13.5 vs 8.2 for the 4B model.](figs/web_spotify-tensorrt-inference/beam_perf.png)

Start with beam search. The test setup is close to generative retrieval: 2,000-token prompts, only 5 generated tokens (a semantic ID string is short), and beam width 30. Read the chart by where the latency curve turns sharply upward; that is where the system can no longer keep up. On the 1.7B model, vLLM loses control around 15 QPS, while TensorRT-LLM holds up to about 33 QPS.

| Workload | Model | TensorRT-LLM saturation | Other engine saturation |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Beam search (vs vLLM) | Qwen3-1.7B | 33.2 QPS | 15.0 QPS |
| Beam search (vs vLLM) | Qwen3-4B | 13.5 QPS | 8.2 QPS |
| Multi-item scoring (vs SGLang) | Qwen3-1.7B | 12.5 ops/s | 12.0 ops/s |
| Multi-item scoring (vs SGLang) | Qwen3-4B | 5.3 ops/s | 4.9 ops/s |

![Figure from the Spotify post: latency and throughput for multi-item scoring, TensorRT-LLM (blue) vs SGLang 0.5.16 (brown), scoring 500 candidates per call with 2,000-token prompts and 10 tokens per candidate. Saturation throughput on the right is nearly equal: 12.5 vs 12.0 for the 1.7B model and 5.3 vs 4.9 for the 4B model.](figs/web_spotify-tensorrt-inference/scoring_perf.png)

Now scoring. With 500 candidates per call, the two engines' saturation throughput is almost the same, with TensorRT-LLM slightly ahead. SGLang was already good at scoring, so the main gain from moving is not speed but no longer maintaining a separate engine.

## Cost

The post's conclusion: on Qwen3-1.7B, beam search workloads cost up to 54% less and scoring workloads up to 7% less. This roughly matches the saturation numbers above: the same card handles more than twice as many beam search requests, so the GPU cost per request falls by about half; scoring throughput is only a few percent higher, so the saving is small.

The indirect gains matter more. In the vLLM days only low-tier cards made sense; once the engine can saturate high-end cards, there is more room in choosing hardware. With all three workloads in one engine, deployment, monitoring and upgrades involve only one stack.

## Limitations as I see them

First, this is a company engineering blog, and the benchmarks run under fixed conditions: 1,000 requests per rate point, a concurrency cap of 64, and unique prompts with no KV cache reuse. In real traffic a user's prefix is often reused, so results may differ; replay your own traffic to check.

Second, the versions and parameters of the compared engines are fixed. vLLM and SGLang move fast and their beam search implementations keep changing, so the gap may shrink in six months. Treat this as a record of where the bottlenecks were at the time, not a final verdict between engines.

Third, scoring currently needs a custom serving layer and soft tokens need a model plugin. For companies without a dedicated inference team, the migration cost is not small.

## How a team could try it

1. List the inference features your generative recommendation needs: multi-beam return, batched candidate scoring, vector injection, and which engine handles each today.
2. Measure beam search saturation QPS with your own prompt length, beam width and decode length. Generative retrieval decodes very little with very wide beams, which is far from chat workloads, so generic benchmarks do not transfer.
3. If you want to give user vectors to the LLM, try soft tokens first: reusing the multimodal vector input path is usually easier than changing the engine core.
4. If scoring already runs well on SGLang, there is no rush to migrate; beam search is the better place to optimize first.

## Bottom line

==Generative recommendation needs different inference from chat: beam search, batched scoring and vector injection are all required. Filling those gaps and unifying them in one engine that saturates the GPU cut beam search cost roughly in half.==

| Dimension | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Importance of the problem | High. Inference cost and engine feature gaps are unavoidable once generative recommendation ships |
| Novelty | Medium. Mostly engineering integration; reusing the multimodal path for soft tokens is worth copying |
| Evidence | Medium. Clear throughput and latency benchmarks, cost reductions from real workloads, but fixed test conditions |
| Engineering cost | Medium-high. Needs a model plugin and a scoring service layer; suits companies with an inference team |
| Worth trying? | Yes. Teams doing semantic-ID generative retrieval with high beam search cost should evaluate it first |

papers.title: BiLoCo: Binary Low-Rank Corrections for Post-Training Quantization
papers.authors: David Jin, Beshr IslamBouli, Tarushii Goel, Han Guo, Yoon Kim
papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) to FP4 has emerged as a key technique for reducing large language model inference cost, especially on Blackwell GPUs, which offer native FP4 tensor core support. Direct PTQ to FP4, however, still leaves a noticeable accuracy gap. Recent work on SVDQuant mitigates the errors introduced through FP4 quantization for diffusion models by adding high-precision low-rank corrections obtained via SVD. However, this high-precision low-rank correction requires many bits per rank, and it runs on the same tensor cores as the main FP4 GEMM. We introduce BiLoCo, a low-rank correction method whose left and right factors are stored as binary ${\{\pm 1\}}$ sign vectors rather than as BF16 numbers. The signed format uses $16{\times}$ less storage per rank-one component, and since the correction now consists of additions/subtractions, this can be run on CUDA cores concurrently with the FP4 tensor-core GEMM. On 4B--72B LLMs, BiLoCo matches or improves memory-matched SVDQuant for PTQ. We implement BiLoCo on B300 as a fused single kernel, where the FP4 GEMM runs on tensor cores, the bit-packed correction on the CUDA cores of the same launch, and the two are combined in the GEMM epilogue. With batch size $1$, the fused kernel is at most $11\%$ slower than the FP4-only GEMM for every rank up to $512$. At rank $128$, it is at most $20\%$ slower up to batch size $8$.

Every vector in the correction is replaced by entries of plus or minus one, so ==the correction needs only additions and subtractions and runs on idle CUDA cores alongside the matrix multiply==. The same storage holds 16 times the rank with equal or better perplexity, and at batch size 1 the whole kernel is only 6% to 11% slower than plain FP4.

deep_reading.title: BiLoCo: Binary Low-Rank Corrections for Post-Training Quantization
deep_reading.content:
Quantizing a trained LLM straight to FP4 lets Blackwell GPUs use native FP4 matrix multiplies, but accuracy drops noticeably. The common fix, SVDQuant, stores an extra BF16 low-rank correction, which costs storage and competes with the main computation for the same tensor cores. This paper from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology proposes BiLoCo (binary low-rank correction): every vector in the correction is replaced by +1 and −1 entries, so applying the correction needs only additions and subtractions and can run on the otherwise idle CUDA cores, concurrently with the FP4 matrix multiply. ==The same storage holds 16 times the rank, perplexity matches or beats SVDQuant on 4B to 72B models, and at batch size 1 the whole kernel is only 6% to 11% slower than plain FP4==.

My take: teams deploying LLM inference and evaluating FP4 should read this. The starting point is practical: during decoding, the matrix multiply is bound by reading weights from memory, the tensor cores wait for data, and the CUDA cores sit idle, so the correction is designed to fit exactly those idle units. The method is simple and the code is public. But it only pays off for small-batch decoding; at larger batches the advantage disappears, so check your serving profile first.

## What problem does it solve?

Post-training quantization (PTQ) means compressing weights and activations to low precision after training, without fine-tuning. Blackwell GPUs natively support NVFP4 matrix multiplies: every 16 values share one FP8 scale and each value has 4 bits, about 4.5 bits per weight on average. Both storage and compute are low precision, so it is cheap.

The trouble is that 4 bits can only represent 15 values: 0, ±0.5, ±1, ±1.5, ±2, ±3, ±4 and ±6. If a block contains a few very large values, the shared scale must accommodate them and everything else in the block loses precision. Quantizing directly to NVFP4 therefore raises perplexity visibly.

A natural fix is to split the weight into two parts: a residual R stored in 4 bits plus a low-rank matrix stored at higher precision, which absorbs the large directions 4 bits cannot represent. SVDQuant does this with a rank-32 BF16 correction obtained by SVD. That correction has two costs: each rank stores two BF16 vectors, which is a lot of bits, and it is itself a matrix multiply that competes with the FP4 computation for tensor cores.

## The core idea: corrections made only of +1 and −1

![Figure 1 from the paper: BiLoCo inference. The top path runs the FP4 matrix multiply on tensor cores, with quantized activations and the residual weight R. The bottom path runs the correction on CUDA cores: a signed sum of the input using the ±1 right vectors V, a scale by coefficients α, and a signed expansion with the ±1 left vectors U. The two results are added in the GEMM epilogue and written out in BF16.](figs/2610.32243/biloco_teaser.png)

BiLoCo writes the correction as a sum of r rank-one terms, each a coefficient α times two vectors containing only +1 and −1. At inference it computes α·u·(v·x). The dot product v·x needs only additions and subtractions: add the matching entry of x where v is +1, subtract it where v is −1.

A worked example: if x is [0.5, −1.2, 2.0, 0.3] and v is [+1, −1, +1, −1], then v·x = 0.5 + 1.2 + 2.0 − 0.3 = 3.4, with no multiplications at all. Multiply by α, then use the signs of u to add or subtract that number into each output position.

The storage arithmetic is favorable. Ignoring the coefficients, a pair of sign vectors costs 1 bit per entry while a pair of BF16 vectors costs 16, so the same storage holds 16 times the rank. For a 5120×5120 matrix, a BF16 rank-32 correction and a binary rank-512 correction both take about 5.2 million bits, while the FP4 weight itself takes about 120 million bits, so the correction adds only about 4% storage.

## Is more rank better than more precise rank?

At equal storage, should you spend bits on a few precise directions or many coarse ones? It depends on the singular value spectrum. If the first few directions dominate, a few precise ranks suffice; if the spectrum is flat, covering more directions matters more.

The authors measured 189 projection matrices from three models and found the leading spectrum is flat: the first singular value is only about twice the 32nd. They measure capture as the ratio of the Frobenius norm of the low-rank part to that of the original matrix. By this measure, binary rank 512 captures 47% to 53%, while BF16 rank 32 captures only 26% to 29%.

![Figure 2 from the paper: on 63 projection matrices of Qwen3-4B, the share of the original matrix captured by the low-rank part (vertical axis) versus storage budget (horizontal axis). Blue is BiLoCo (binary rank equal to the budget), red is SVDQuant (BF16 rank equal to budget divided by 16), at equal storage. Blue is higher at every budget, by 24.2 points at budget 512.](figs/2610.32243/capture_vs_rank.png)

At every storage budget the binary correction captures more. On LLM weights, spending limited storage on covering more directions beats making each direction more precise.

## Finding the sign vectors

The optimal binary decomposition cannot be read off an SVD. The authors use an existing greedy procedure that finds one rank-one component at a time:

1. Set the residual R to the original weight W.
2. Initialize a random sign vector v and alternate: u takes the signs of Rv, v takes the signs of Rᵀu. Five rounds are enough to settle.
3. Compute the error-minimizing coefficient α, subtract α·u·vᵀ from the residual, and find the next component.
4. After all components are found, refit all coefficients jointly, because components overlap and individually fitted coefficients are not optimal.
5. Quantize what remains of the residual to NVFP4.

It is fast: at rank 512, one B300 handles Qwen3-4B in about 1 minute and Qwen3-32B in about 5 minutes.

## How the kernel adds almost no time

Additions alone are not enough; the correction must truly overlap the FP4 multiply. The authors wrote a fused kernel for the B300, which has 148 streaming multiprocessors (SMs, the GPU's independently scheduled compute units).

At launch, some thread blocks run the FP4 multiply as usual, each owning one 128×64 output tile. The remaining thread blocks compute the intermediate z = α·(v·x) on CUDA cores and write it to a small buffer in memory. The epilogue threads of each GEMM block, which are idle during the main loop anyway, wait for z, expand it with u into the correction for their tile, and add it before writing the result. Compared with running the GEMM and then launching a separate correction kernel, this uses a single launch, no extra stream, and no write-out and read-back of the full output; the only extra memory traffic is the tiny z buffer.

Why does the correction cost so little? It reads very little data. At rank 128 it reads about 0.16 MiB of sign bits while the FP4 path reads about 12.5 MiB of weights, an 80x gap. Because data reading is nearly free, the correction's time is set by four steps that must happen in order: accumulate the signed sums over the input dimension, publish z to the buffer, have the GEMM block wait until z is ready, and expand with u. As long as these finish before the GEMM main loop ends, the correction is fully hidden.

## Result one: accuracy

| Model | BF16 | Direct NVFP4 | SVDQuant rank 32 | BiLoCo rank 512 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Qwen3-4B | 14.22 | 15.13 | 15.07 | 14.94 |
| Llama-3-8B | 6.27 | 7.00 | 6.92 | 6.84 |
| Qwen3-14B | 8.89 | 9.36 | 9.19 | 9.17 |
| Qwen3-32B | 7.85 | 8.23 | 8.18 | 8.16 |
| Qwen2.5-72B | 3.92 | 4.29 | 4.23 | 4.23 |

The table shows WikiText-2 perplexity (lower is better), with BiLoCo and SVDQuant at equal storage. On 4B, 8B and 14B BiLoCo is better on both WikiText-2 and C4; on 32B and 72B it ties or is slightly better. With a quarter of the storage (rank 128), BiLoCo trails SVDQuant by at most 0.05.

Perplexity gaps look small; the distance to the original model's output distribution says more. The authors computed per-token KL divergence between each quantized model and the BF16 model on 200 FineWeb documents, reporting both the mean and the 99th percentile, the value at the 99% position when all token KLs are sorted. BiLoCo has a lower 99th-percentile KL on all five models; on Qwen3-14B it is 0.130 versus 0.167, 22% lower. So the gain is not just on typical tokens but larger on the tokens most likely to go wrong.

Downstream gains are much smaller: compared with SVDQuant at equal storage, mean WinoGrande and HellaSwag accuracy is 0.1 to 0.7 points higher on the four Qwen models and 0.3 points lower on Llama-3-8B.

## Result two: speed

The test shape is K = N = 5120, close to an attention projection in a 14B model, compared against the fastest plain FP4 kernel measured in the same run.

| Batch size | Extra time at rank 128 | Extra time at rank 512 |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | 8% | 11% |
| 2 | 8% | 15% |
| 4 | 11% | 44% |
| 8 | 15% | 74% |
| 16 | 55% | 204% |

At batch 1, every rank from 16 to 512 adds 6% to 11%, or 0.34 to 0.64 microseconds. But correction work grows with both batch and rank, while FP4 GEMM time barely changes up to batch 128 because it is spent reading weights. So larger batches expose the correction. With a 20% overhead limit, rank 128 works up to batch 8 and rank 512 only up to batch 2.

One easy-to-miss result: a dense BF16 correction of the same rank inside the same kernel takes the same time as the binary one. The advantage of the binary format is not faster arithmetic but more rank per byte.

## Limitations as I see them

First, the scope is narrow. It only pays off for small-batch decoding; if your service often runs at batch 16 or more, overhead doubles or worse, and the authors themselves recommend a tensor-core correction there.

Second, the kernel does not support the MLP gate and up projections. Those layers are so wide that they need more output tiles than the B300 has SMs, while the kernel requires all GEMM blocks to run at once. These are exactly the largest layers, so end-to-end speedups need another solution for them.

Third, speed is measured only per kernel, with no end-to-end decode latency for a full model. The accuracy gains are also modest: downstream tasks differ by fractions of a point, and the clearest perplexity gains are on smaller models.

## How a team could try it

1. Confirm your deployment is small-batch decoding, such as on-device, low-concurrency private deployment, or latency-sensitive single-user serving.
2. Quantize your model with the public code; it takes minutes. Check perplexity and KL against direct NVFP4.
3. If accuracy improves meaningfully, time the kernel over your usual batch range and pick a rank within 20% overhead.
4. For gate and up projections, keep an SVDQuant-style correction or plain quantization, and use BiLoCo for the other layers.

## Bottom line

==During decoding the tensor cores wait on memory while the CUDA cores sit idle; making the FP4 correction out of ±1 vectors that need only additions buys 16 times the rank for the same storage at almost no extra time at small batch sizes.==

|---|---|
| Problem importance | Medium-high. FP4 is the main lever for cheaper inference on Blackwell, and its accuracy loss blocks adoption |
| Novelty | Medium. The decomposition reuses prior work; the novelty is matching the correction format to idle hardware |
| Evidence | Medium. Perplexity, KL and downstream tasks on 5 models plus kernel timing; no end-to-end latency |
| Engineering cost | Medium. Code is public and quantization takes minutes; the fused kernel needs a B300 and does not cover all layers |
| Worth trying | Yes for teams deploying FP4 on Blackwell for small-batch decoding |

papers.title: GS-MoE: Training-Free MoE Compression via Groupwise Subspace Sharing and Pruning
papers.authors: Carson Cary, Yukai Jin, Yihao Huang, Zhankai Ye, Fangyi Li, Ting Hua, Xin Liu, Shangqian Gao
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models reduce computation through sparse activation, but storing their expert parameters remains a major memory bottleneck. We introduce GS-MoE, a training-free compression framework that addresses redundancy across and within experts through two compression axes: shared-subspace rank and expert intermediate width. Groupwise low-rank representations capture shared structure across experts while retaining expert-specific projections, and Nyström-based neuron compression reduces intermediate width within each expert. For fixed shared subspaces, we derive per-expert reconstruction-error reductions from the reconstruction objective and use them to guide expert grouping. Budgets are allocated hierarchically using a gradient-free layer-importance score to guide the allocation of rank and width budgets across layers, which eigenvalues and leverage then distribute as non-uniform ranks across groups and intermediate widths across experts. Experiments demonstrate the complementary benefits of compression along both axes, particularly at high compression rates on fine-grained MoE models. On DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base, at a 60% reduction in total model parameters, GS-MoE retains approximately 90% of the uncompressed model's average reasoning performance, compared with 73% for D$^2$-MoE, while achieving 20% lower out-of-domain perplexity. We provide a code implementation at: https://github.com/cbacary/GS-MoE
papers.summary: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models activate only a few experts per token, so compute is cheap, but every expert's parameters must stay in GPU memory, and memory is usually the first thing that blocks deployment. This paper proposes GS-MoE, which needs no retraining and compresses experts along two axes at once. First, similar experts are grouped, and ==each group shares one input and one output projection while each expert keeps only a small private matrix==. Second, intermediate neurons inside each expert that other neurons can stand in for are removed. On DeepSeek-MoE-16B with 60% of parameters removed, average accuracy on reasoning tasks stays at about 90% of the original model, versus 73% for the baseline D2-MoE.

deep_reading.title: GS-MoE: Training-Free MoE Compression via Groupwise Subspace Sharing and Pruning
deep_reading.content:
Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models activate only a few experts per token, so compute is cheap, but every expert's parameters must stay in GPU memory, and memory is usually the first thing that blocks deployment. This paper proposes GS-MoE, which needs no retraining and compresses experts along two axes at once: similar experts are grouped and share one input and one output projection per group, with each expert keeping only a small private matrix; and inside each expert, unimportant intermediate neurons are removed, with the kept neurons used to approximate what the removed ones contributed. ==On DeepSeek-MoE-16B with 60% of parameters removed, average accuracy on 7 reasoning tasks stays at about 90% of the original model, versus 73% for the baseline D2-MoE==.

My take: teams deploying fine-grained MoE models (many small experts, such as the DeepSeek and Qwen2 MoE models) on memory-constrained machines should look at this. It needs one forward pass to collect statistics and one GPU to compress, and the code is public, so the cost is low. Two caveats: it does not win on Mixtral, which has few large experts; and the paper's own breakdown shows most of the gain comes from the neuron-removal half, while the group-sharing half adds little in most settings.

## What problem does it solve?

An MoE model replaces a feed-forward layer with dozens of parallel experts, and a router picks a few for each token. DeepSeek-MoE-16B has 64 experts per layer and uses 6 per token. Compute drops, but the other 58 experts must remain in memory because the next token may need them.

Existing compression methods fall into roughly three types. The first removes or merges whole experts, and quality drops quickly as more are removed. The second makes all experts share one low-rank basis, as in MoE-SVD; but with one shared subspace per layer, any direction unique to an expert that falls outside it can never be represented. The third is D2-MoE, which stores one shared base weight plus a compressed difference per expert, again tying the whole layer together. There are also methods that only remove neurons inside experts, which ignore what experts have in common, so each expert still stores its own weights.

The authors' starting point: similarity among experts is not layer-wide but local, with some experts resembling each other. So experts should first be grouped, share within the group, use different subspaces across groups, and have their internal redundancy compressed too.

## Method: group sharing plus neuron removal

![Figure 1 from the paper: the structure of GS-MoE. Left is an uncompressed expert with one up projection and one down projection. Right, after compression, experts are split into G equal-size groups; each group shares an input projection P↑ and an output projection P↓, and each expert keeps only its own small matrices A↑ and A↓. Hatched cells are removed parts: different groups have different shared dimensions, and different experts keep different numbers of neurons.](figs/2610.32009/GS-MoE-Method.png)

After compression an expert computes in four steps: the input is multiplied by the group's shared input projection into a lower dimension. Then it is multiplied by the expert's own small matrix to get the kept intermediate activations. After the activation function, the expert's other small matrix maps it back to the low dimension. Finally it is multiplied by the group's shared output projection back to the model dimension. Memory savings come from two places: shared projections are stored once per group, and private matrices are small because both sides shrink.

There are four stages.

First, neuron selection. The authors run calibration data through the original model, record statistics of each expert's intermediate activations, and score each neuron with a ridge leverage score that measures how irreplaceable it is: a neuron whose activation is well represented by a combination of other neurons scores low and can be removed. All neurons of all experts in a layer are ranked together and the top K are kept, so different experts keep different widths. K is set by the overall budget, described in the fourth stage.

Second, fitting projections. The output side has a closed-form solution: sum the output covariances of the experts in the group, and the leading eigenvectors form the shared output projection. The input side has none, because experts see different input distributions. The authors average the group's input covariances, weighted by the number of tokens routed to each expert, and treat that as the group's input distribution. The goal is that after the low-dimensional projection, each expert's pre-activation values for its kept neurons can still be reconstructed. Under the averaged distribution this has an approximate solution. For each expert, take the kept rows of its up projection and compute their transpose times themselves, a model-dimension square matrix (so different kept widths do not change its size). Sum these with token weights, multiply on both sides by the square root of the averaged input covariance, take the leading eigenvectors, multiply by the inverse square root and orthonormalize. With the shared projection fixed, each expert's private matrix is a least-squares fit on that expert's own input covariance. Removed neurons are compensated with the Nyström approximation, a classic method for reconstructing a full covariance matrix from a few kept columns: from the recorded intermediate-activation covariance, compute a linear map that predicts the full intermediate activation from the kept neurons, and fold that map into the private down matrix. The down projection then reads only kept neurons yet approximates the contribution of all of them.

Third, grouping. The authors derive a score for how much an expert's reconstruction error drops inside a candidate subspace. They fit a subspace for each expert alone, then put expert i into expert j's subspace, reconstruct expert i's kept pre-activations and outputs, add the two errors (the output term is scaled by the fraction of up-projection output energy retained after neuron removal, to balance the two terms), and measure the drop from the no-reconstruction error. Dividing by the drop expert i gets in its own subspace gives a ratio; one minus it is the dissimilarity. With a 64×64 dissimilarity matrix, balanced clustering produces equal-size groups.

Fourth, capacity allocation. Each layer gets an importance score: for each token routed to an expert, the expert's output norm times the routing weight divided by the input norm, averaged over that expert's tokens and summed over the layer's experts. The target compression ratio gives the overall retained fraction R of expert parameters; a hyperparameter ν (0.45 to 0.55 by default) sets the width retention to R to the power ν, and the shared-dimension retention follows as R divided by the width retention plus the shared-projection overhead. Removal is spread across layers by a softmax over negative log importance, so less important layers lose more. Within a layer, eigenvalue sums decide each group's shared dimension under the layer budget.

The whole process takes one forward pass over 512 Alpaca samples of 2048 tokens each, fits on one GPU, and involves no training afterward.

## Does grouping actually help?

![Figure 2(c) from the paper: pairwise dissimilarity among the 64 experts of DeepSeek-MoE-16B layer 22; darker means more similar. The horizontal axis is the subspace fitted to each expert, the vertical axis the expert evaluated, and white boxes are the final 8 groups. Inside the boxes colors are clearly darker, so grouped experts really do share subspaces well; a few rows are bright throughout, experts that resemble no one.](figs/2610.32009/deepseek-l22-dissim.png)

The authors ablated this on DeepSeek-MoE-16B at 60% compression using only group sharing, without neuron removal. Without grouping, WikiText-2 perplexity is 29.49; with score-based grouping it falls to 25.23, because similar experts lose less when sharing a subspace. Adding per-group dimension allocation lowers it a further 0.57 on average across three datasets. Without grouping, dimension allocation alone brings no consistent gain.

Grouping has a side benefit: if a token's selected experts fall in the same group, the shared projection is computed once. With 8 groups each token touches only 3.68 groups on average, about 19% fewer than random grouping.

## Results

The authors compare against MoE-SVD, D2-MoE, TD-MoE and others on three models, using average accuracy over 7 zero-shot reasoning tasks and perplexity on WikiText-2 and PTB (another language-modeling test set). Compression ratio is the reduction in total model parameters.

| Model and ratio | Original | D2-MoE | GS-MoE |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| DeepSeek-MoE-16B, 40% | 0.56 | 0.49 | 0.54 |
| DeepSeek-MoE-16B, 60% | 0.56 | 0.41 | 0.50 |
| Qwen2-57B-A14B, 40% | 0.59 | 0.58 | 0.59 |
| Mixtral-8x7B, 40% | 0.63 | 0.57 | 0.57 |
| Mixtral-8x7B, 60% | 0.63 | 0.52 | 0.50 |

On the two fine-grained models GS-MoE leads clearly: 0.50 versus 0.41 on DeepSeek at 60%; Qwen2 at 60% still averages 0.59, equal to the original, while the next best, TD-MoE, reaches 0.52. On Mixtral, with only 8 large experts, it ties D2-MoE and is slightly worse at 60%, which suggests the advantage comes from many fine-grained experts.

Perplexity is more mixed. On DeepSeek at 60%, GS-MoE scores 22.21 on PTB versus 27.73 for D2-MoE, 20% lower, which is the source of the abstract's out-of-domain claim; but on WikiText-2 it scores 17.55, clearly worse than D2-MoE's 11.67. Which method is better depends on the metric you look at.

## Limitations as I see them

First, the two halves contribute unevenly. The appendix tests group sharing only and neuron removal only: on Qwen2 and Mixtral, neuron removal alone is nearly as good as the full method; only on DeepSeek at 60% is the full method clearly better (0.503 versus 0.487). In many settings, Nyström neuron removal alone gets most of the gain.

Second, it does not suit models with few large experts. The authors acknowledge that Mixtral's large intermediate size and 8 experts make lowering the subspace dimension more damaging and leave little to group.

Third, evaluation covers only language modeling and multiple-choice reasoning, with no generation, long context or code, and no combination with quantization. In practice MoE deployments more often quantize or offload rarely used experts to CPU memory; the paper does not compare against those.

1. Confirm your model is a fine-grained MoE with around 64 experts or more.
2. Run only the neuron-removal part first and measure the loss at 40% compression on your own evaluation set; it is the cheapest step.
3. To reach around 60%, add group sharing and check generation quality, not just perplexity.
4. Increase the number of groups gradually and measure throughput at each step, since more groups mean more shared projections and slightly lower speed.

papers.title: HyScale: Scaling Long-Context Training for Learned Sparse Attention
papers.authors: Yangsheng Deng, Xinjing Huang, Yulong Wang, Yunzhuo Liu, Jun Hu, Shuyong Tang, Junchi Zeng, Mingji Han, Ray Ying, Key Zhang, Luo Mai
papers.abstract: We present HyScale, a long-context training system for learned sparse attention. Learned sparse attention is a promising architecture for million-token contexts, widely adopted in production since DeepSeek-V3.2. Selection, however, grows into the training bottleneck. For each query, it scores every previous token whereas sparse attention reads only $k$; worse, current systems materialize a full score table and repeat selection during recomputation. Our key insight is that the output of selection is not an activation, but rather a set of indices. Building on it, HyScale introduces HyTopK and selection replay. HyTopK finds each query's exact top-$k$ on the fly without a score table, while selection replay reuses forward-pass selection in recomputation. Together with holistic system optimizations tackling end-to-end training challenges, HyScale speeds up GLM-5.1 training on 1M-token sequences by 2.07$\times$ over Megatron-LM on 512 H20 GPUs. It also speeds up the CSA layers of DeepSeek-V4-Flash and the QSA layers of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next by 2.01$\times$ and 1.57$\times$ at 1M tokens on 32 H800 GPUs.
papers.summary: Learned sparse attention lets each query read only the k most relevant earlier tokens and is a popular architecture for million-token contexts. But the selection step that picks those k tokens scores every earlier token, and in training it becomes the bottleneck, taking nearly half of each step on long sequences in Megatron-LM. HyScale's key observation is that ==selection outputs only a set of indices, so there is no need to store a full score table or to select again during recomputation==. It finds the exact top k on the fly and reuses the forward-pass indices during recomputation. Training million-token sequences on 512 H20 GPUs, it runs 2.07x faster end to end than Megatron-LM.

papers.title: Nested Sparsity for Scalable Pretraining and Continual Learning
papers.authors: Tianzhe Chu, Druv Pai, Yi Ma
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) transformers, the standard backbone for modern large-scale deep learning, employ conditional computation: only a sparse subset of model weights is used in each forward pass. In MoE transformers, this sparsity arises in the MoE operator, which generalizes the multi-layer perceptron in the classical transformer. In this work, we explore an alternative mechanism for conditional computation that analogously generalizes the attention operator. The sparsity induced by this mechanism naturally nests (i.e., hierarchically composes) with the sparsity induced by the MoE operator. We show that a transformer employing this nested sparsity mechanism, which we call Nestor, performs better than a conventional MoE transformer at equal compute and equal sparsity in language model pretraining. We also show that Nestor is well-suited for continual pretraining: it can be adapted to longer contexts more effectively than conventional MoEs, as well as adapt more efficiently to new domains while forgetting less on old domains. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these benefits persist as model size, dataset size, and context length grow. Our results demonstrate the potential of alternative conditional computation mechanisms for deep neural network architectures. Code and checkpoints are available on GitHub at https://github.com/Ma-Lab-Berkeley/Nestor .
papers.summary: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models make only the feed-forward layer sparse, while attention still shares one set of parameters across all tokens and sees the full context. This paper proposes Nestor, which also splits attention into several independently parameterized attention modules called columns. A router picks a few columns per token, and ==each column computes attention only among tokens routed to it, with its own set of experts==. Scaling-law experiments show that a standard MoE at equal sparsity needs 13% to 29% more training compute to reach Nestor's held-out loss, and the gap does not shrink as models grow. In continual training on new domains, it learns about as much as an MoE while forgetting less.

papers.title: Efficient Omni-modal Large Language Model Inference via Per-Query Modality Selection
papers.authors: Shuqi Liu, Yuzhou Cao, Luke Ong
papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) can jointly process a broad range of modalities, such as text, audio, and video, enabling stronger multimodal understanding and reasoning capabilities, but often at substantial inference cost. We observe that the benefit of additional modalities varies across queries, indicating that a fixed modality configuration can be inefficient. Motivated by this, we study query-wise modality selection, which keeps the underlying Omni-LLM fixed while adaptively selecting which modalities to provide for each query. We formulate the problem as an accuracy-cost optimization problem and develop a cost-sensitive learning approach for modality selection. We evaluate our approach on WorldSense using Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni under three inference-cost measures: input tokens, latency, and monetary cost. Across both models, query-wise modality selection consistently improves the accuracy-cost trade-off and can even outperform the standard setting in which all available modalities are provided to the Omni-LLM. For Qwen2.5-Omni, our cost-sensitive approach matches or exceeds this full-modality accuracy while requiring only approximately 41% of the input tokens, 39% of the latency, and 61% of the monetary cost.
papers.summary: Omni-modal LLMs can read text, hear audio and watch video together, but video is expensive. On the WorldSense benchmark, text and audio take about three thousand input tokens per question, and adding video raises that to about forty thousand. Many questions do not need the video at all. This paper leaves the model unchanged and decides, per question, which modalities to feed it, ==learning that choice as a trade-off between accuracy and cost==. The selector is a single linear layer that reads only the BGE-M3 embedding of the question text and decides whether to add video; its training objective is the error loss plus a weighted inference cost. On Qwen2.5-Omni, it matches or beats feeding every modality while using only about 41% of the input tokens and 39% of the latency.

papers.title: Tensormesh Launches Tensormesh Platform to Cut LLM Inference Costs by Reusing KV Cache at Enterprise Scale
papers.abstract: This multi-tier, scalable KV cache management software deploys across infrastructure with an enterprise Kubernetes deployment.
papers.summary: LLM inference keeps recomputing the same context, wasting GPU time and delaying the first token. Tensormesh, the team behind the open-source KV cache project LMCache, has launched an enterprise product, Tensormesh Platform, that ==runs KV cache as a managed data layer==. It caches automatically across GPU memory, host memory and storage, reuses both prompt prefixes and, through CacheBlend, chunks in the middle of a prompt, which suits retrieval-augmented generation. Machines in a cluster can also fetch KV cache directly from each other. The platform deploys on the company's own Kubernetes cluster and adds production features such as data security, real-time monitoring, high availability, cache policies and multi-tenant isolation.

papers.title: Kolibri: A Sovereign European Model on the Pareto Frontier

Burns, Björn Deiseroth, Niko Dürr, Béni Balázs Egressy, Niklas Finken, Niklas Freymuth, Fabian Gebhart, Max Hammer, Bastian Harren, Andreas Hartel, Johann Higl, Steffen Hirschmann, Pablo Iyu Guerrero, Yasser Jadidi, Andreas Jagusch, Mitja Kleider, Markus Klein, Jonas Knupp, Murali Kondragunta, Garwin Lechner, Dominik Lê-Kellner, Jurek Leonhardt, Jiaze Li, Sohir Maskey, Omar Mehio, Pit Neitemeier, Letitia Parcalabescu, Alejandro Petry Pacheco, Pranav Ragupathy, Martin Reinhardt, Peter Rodenkirch Nfissi, Dylan Rodriquez, Leonard Salewski, Raziye Sari, Jordan Sassoon, Ivo Schaper, Ilhan Scheer, Frank Schneider, Philipp Scholl, Lukas Schott, Eric Schreiber, Pablo Schumacher, Alessio Serra, Philipp Siedler, Prabhu Teja Sivaprasad, Mohamed Soliman, Till Speicher, Volker Stampa, Simon Thel, Serge Thilges, Irina Vidal Migallón, Denis Waßmann, Samuel Weinbach, Sascha Wirges, Michael Wüthrich, Alexei Zacharov
papers.abstract: This report introduces Kolibri, an English-German mixture-of-experts transformer with 78.1B total parameters and 3.46B active parameters per token, released as open weights under the Apache 2.0 licence. We built Kolibri for sovereign and specialised deployment, with a particular focus on German and on regulated domains such as public administration, industry, and aerospace. To support these settings, we control the full model-development process, including data, architecture, training infrastructure, post-training, and evaluation. We train Kolibri on 24T tokens across pre-training, mid-training, and long-context extension, with German accounting for more than 20% of the data mix by bytes. To reach this share, we complement German datasets with more than 2T German tokens that we curate from the web with our own pipeline and generate synthetically. Post-training combines supervised fine-tuning on curated German and English data with reinforcement learning on more than 1.2M internally curated tasks, which cover reasoning, tool use, instruction following, code, and retrieval. The model activates 4.4% of its parameters per token, and among the open models evaluated in this report, it lies on the Pareto frontier of quality and serving cost in English and German. Kolibri builds on Kolibri Origin, an earlier iteration that validated our full pipeline at scale. Both models come from our Model Factory, which connects data, experimentation, training, evaluation, and deployment through version-controlled workflows.
papers.summary: Regulated European sectors such as public administration, industry and aerospace need open models they can control and that handle German well. Kolibri is an English-German mixture-of-experts model with 78.1 billion total parameters and about 3.5 billion active per token, released as open weights. ==The team controls the whole process, from data and architecture to training infrastructure, post-training and evaluation==, and built its own pipeline to curate and synthesize more than 2 trillion German tokens so that German makes up a large share of training data. Among the open models compared in the report, it sits on the quality and serving-cost frontier in both English and German, meaning the best quality at its cost.

papers.title: 人工智能平台 PAI：模型蒸馏（ModelDistill）
papers.abstract: PAI 模型蒸馏（ModelDistill）提供一站式的模型蒸馏服务，支持通用蒸馏和多种场景化蒸馏模板。
papers.summary: If you want to move a large model's ability into a cheaper small model without building the pipeline yourself, ModelDistill, the model distillation service on Alibaba Cloud's PAI platform, offers it as a no-code managed service. It uses black-box distillation: ==the teacher model generates high-quality training data, and the student model is trained on it with SFT==, using LoRA, QLoRA or full fine-tuning. Besides general templates, it offers scenario templates for instruction following, chain-of-thought reasoning, agent tool calling, text-to-video and coding agents. The documentation also warns that distillation always loses some quality, and for simple classification or text matching, fine-tuning a small model directly may be cheaper.
